title: India Tells Meta to Follow Indian Law, Not Just Its Own Global Policies
excerpt: The Indian government has told Meta that its platforms must comply with the country's laws and cannot operate solely under the company's internal global policies, following weeks of escalating confrontations over content moderation failures.
body:
• Indian government sources told ANI that Meta's platforms must comply with Indian law, not merely the company's global policies.
  • The directive follows Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's apology over child sexual abuse material and CEO Joel Kaplan's apology for restricting PM Modi's Facebook post.
  • India has tightened content takedown rules from 36 hours to 3 hours and summoned Meta's global executives to New Delhi for accountability discussions.
  • A parliamentary panel and the Supreme Court have separately intensified scrutiny of Meta's operations in India.

India's government has told Meta Platforms that its social media services must comply with Indian law and cannot be governed solely by the company's global policies, news agency ANI reported on Sunday, quoting government sources.

The statement marks the latest escalation in a weeks-long confrontation between New Delhi and the Mark Zuckerberg-led company over content moderation, child safety and platform accountability in India — Meta's largest market by user count.

From Apologies to Accountability

The government's stance follows a series of meetings between Meta executives and officials from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). On August 5, Meta's Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan apologised to India's IT minister for briefly restricting a post by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in July, calling it an operational error, according to Reuters.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2086349496292987122

"I apologised to the minister on behalf of Meta for the error restricting PM Modi's post."

— Joel Kaplan, Meta Chief Global Affairs Officer

Separately, Zuckerberg himself apologised to the Indian government over child sexual abuse material, deepfake content and other operational lapses on Meta's platforms, according to Moneycontrol and other Indian media outlets. The apology came during a meeting between Meta executives and government officials on the same day.

MeitY had summoned Meta's global team after Facebook briefly restricted Modi's July 23 post — a selfie video addressed to India's youth promising action against examination paper leaks. Meta attributed the removal to an AI-powered content filter glitch, but the ministry found the explanation "inadequate."

Tighter Rules, Higher Stakes

India has significantly toughened its regulatory framework for tech platforms this year. The government compressed the timeline for removing content flagged by authorities from 36 hours to just three hours — a compliance challenge for Meta, YouTube and X alike.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=T7KCfhgr_4s

In March, New Delhi proposed making government advisories legally binding on internet platforms. Under the proposed rules, non-compliance would strip platforms of their safe harbour protection — the legal shield that protects them from liability for user-posted content.

The government also ordered Meta to remove advertisements and content promoting child sexual abuse material on Instagram in July, following a BBC investigation that found Meta's recommendation algorithm had been promoting such content. Government sources said Meta must clarify issues around algorithmic bias and its role in maintaining public order.

Courts Add Pressure

The judiciary has piled on. India's Supreme Court warned Meta in February: "If you can't follow our Constitution, leave India. We won't allow citizens' privacy to be compromised." The court was hearing appeals against a ₹213.14 crore ($25.4 million) penalty imposed by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) over WhatsApp's 2021 privacy policy.

WhatsApp subsequently agreed to comply with directions mandating user consent for data sharing with other Meta entities, withdrawing key parts of its challenge before the Supreme Court.

Meanwhile, police in Hyderabad registered a case against Meta India head Arun Srinivas over videos posted on Facebook that allegedly depicted Modi in an "abusive manner," Reuters reported.

What This Means for India's Tech Landscape

For the Indian diaspora and NRIs who rely on WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook to stay connected with family and communities in India, the regulatory push signals a shift in how these platforms will operate in the country. Stricter data-sharing consent requirements and faster content moderation could reshape the user experience.

A parliamentary panel has also summoned representatives of Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, along with MeitY and Home Affairs officials, to discuss social media regulation. The agenda covers user safety, privacy protections and the role of platforms in maintaining public order.

What's Next

Meta's global team is expected in New Delhi in the coming days for further discussions with government officials. The company faces the challenge of balancing its global operational framework with India's increasingly assertive regulatory demands — while managing fallout from a $942 million child safety ruling in New Mexico and over $1 trillion in potential damages from lawsuits by U.S. state attorneys general.
